issues.legal_issue: Semi-digested food in a deceased person’s stomach does not, by itself, discredit eyewitness testimony about the time of an attack when stomach contents cannot reliably establish the time of death or eating.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses said that the family had eaten shortly before the attack.
The post-mortem examination found semi-digested food in the deceased’s stomach.
The Court noted that stomach contents cannot be determined with precision at the time of death.
issues.conclusion: The medical observation did not contradict the eyewitness account strongly enough to discredit it.
issues.legal_principle: Medical evidence about stomach contents cannot precisely establish the time of death or eating, and an uncertain medical observation should not displace otherwise reliable eyewitness testimony. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this evidentiary principle.

predicates.appeal_after_reversal_of_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal following a conviction entered after an earlier acquittal was reversed.
predicates.eyewitnesses_describe_recent_meal: Eyewitnesses said that the deceased and others ate shortly before the attack.
predicates.stomach_contents_are_semi_digested: A medical examination found semi-digested food in the deceased’s stomach.
predicates.stomach_contents_cannot_fix_timing: The medical evidence does not allow the time of eating or death to be determined precisely.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed, eyewitnesses describe a recent meal, and semi-digested stomach contents cannot establish timing precisely, the timing account is not discredited on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an independent witness and minor variations among eyewitness accounts do not discredit testimony when the witnesses’ presence is supported and the account is otherwise reliable.
material_facts: The three eyewitnesses were at or near the place of the occurrence, and the Court found their presence could not be doubted.
One eyewitness was injured, and medical evidence supported her account of those injuries.
A prompt report contained details of the occurrence.
The witnesses differed on some details, including the precise place where they had been sitting, the location of the light, and the manner in which injuries were inflicted.
No independent witness testified about the occurrence or the accused’s movements.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an independent witness and the variations identified did not justify rejecting the eyewitness testimony; the variations were insignificant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the eyewitnesses’ supported presence, the injured witness’s corroborated injuries, and the prompt report as grounds for accepting their account. It held that witnesses to a violent event need not each recount every injury in the same sequence and that insignificant variations do not undermine the account. It cited no provision or earlier case for these principles.

predicates.appeal_after_reversal_of_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal following a conviction entered after an earlier acquittal was reversed.
predicates.eyewitness_presence_supported: Circumstances in the record support the eyewitnesses’ presence at the occurrence.
predicates.injured_witness_medically_supported: Medical evidence supports the account of injuries sustained by an eyewitness during the occurrence.
predicates.prompt_detailed_report: A report was made promptly and included details of the occurrence.
predicates.discrepancies_are_insignificant: Differences among witnesses concern details that do not undermine the central account of the occurrence.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed, the eyewitnesses’ presence and an injured witness’s account are supported, a detailed report was prompt, and differences are insignificant, the absence of independent witnesses and those differences do not discredit the testimony.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction entered after reversal of an acquittal is sustainable when the eyewitness evidence establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the acquittal rested on unsound or insignificant considerations.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, relying principally on its interpretation of semi-digested food, discrepancies about the place and lighting, variations in descriptions of the injuries, and the evidence of motive.
The High Court reassessed the eyewitness evidence and convicted the accused.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitnesses’ presence credible, the injured witness’s presence medically supported, and the report prompt and detailed.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s view perverse and concluded that the eyewitness evidence established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and left in place the convictions under Sections 302/34 and 323/34 of the Indian Penal Code, including the individual conviction under Section 323.
issues.legal_principle: In the appeal brought under Section 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, the Court upheld the convictions under Sections 302/34 and 323/34 of the Indian Penal Code because the evidence established guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the trial court’s contrary view was perverse. The Court cited no earlier case.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_after_reversal_of_a: The proceeding is a Supreme Court appeal concerning convictions entered after a higher court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.eyewitness_evidence_establishes_guilt_be: Credible eyewitness evidence establishes the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.acquittal_rest_ed_on_unsound_inferences: The earlier acquittal rested on inferences that are perverse or on insignificant considerations.

issues.definition: When a Supreme Court appeal concerns convictions entered after an acquittal was reversed, credible eyewitness evidence establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the acquittal rested on unsound inferences, the conviction is upheld.
